KEY MESSAGE 1...Cloudy and cooler conditions are expected through
mid-week, along with daily chances for showers.

Conditions will turn out mostly cloudy today. Temperatures will
be cooler than previous days, and conditions will also be less 
humid, with dewpoints dropping into the 60s. There could be a 
substantial gradient in temperatures from northwest to southeast
today. Western Maryland and the West Virginia Panhandle will 
likely struggle to climb out of the 60s with thick cloud cover 
and higher coverage of showers. Locations along and east of I-95
may make it into the upper 70s to near 80 with lower coverage 
of showers and a few more breaks in the cloud cover.

High pressure already in place to our north across southern
Quebec will rapidly strengthen from the upper 1020s hPa today 
to near 1040 hPa by tomorrow night. As this occurs, 
northeasterly flow will strengthen and the CAD wedge in place 
to the east of the Appalachians will strengthen. Large scale 
forcing for ascent will also gradually increase from west to 
east tonight into tomorrow as a shortwave trough and embedded 
upper low approach from the Ohio Valley. As large scale forcing 
for ascent increases, the relatively low coverage of showers 
today will increase substantially heading into tonight, and 
persist through tomorrow, tomorrow night, and Wednesday morning.
At times, the precipitation may even resemble more of a 
continuous stratiform rain shield as opposed to showers.

The flow pattern across the CONUS over the next couple days will
be extremely complex, with a split flow pattern and a closed 
upper-level ridge building to the north of the upper low over 
the Ohio Valley. So while the big picture of the forecast 
tonight through Wednesday has high confidence (low clouds, cool,
and rainy), there is still some forecast uncertainty regarding 
the finer scale details. A few model solutions attempt to 
produce several inches of rainfall over localized areas as we 
become positioned in the right entrance region of a strong jet 
streak developing off to our north and east, but there is lots 
of model to model inconsistency as to if that will occur and 
where. As of now, the most likely scenario appears to be for 
most of the region to receive 1-2 inches of rainfall spread out 
over a prolonged period time tonight through Wednesday morning.
If this were to occur, the rainfall would be beneficial in 
nature given the ongoing drought conditions. However, if the 
solutions that produce isolated totals of 3-6 inches were to 
play out, there could be localized issues with flooding. Even if
the solution with higher end totals plays out, instantaneous 
rainfall rates won't be overly high given the lack of 
instability, so it would be more of a prolonged soaking rainfall
leading to areal flooding, as opposed to thunderstorms 
producing flash flooding. We'll continue to monitor this 
potential as we move forward.

Either way, Tuesday and Wednesday will feature low clouds, 
gusty northeasterly winds, and well below normal temperatures. 
Temperatures likely hold in the 60s on Tuesday, and may even 
struggle to get out of the 50s on Wednesday as the CAD wedge 
reaches its peak strength.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Daily shower chances, abundant cloud cover, and cool
temperatures continue through Thursday. Drier this weekend.

A persistent wedge-like pattern will remain through at least 
Thursday as wedging/blocking high pressure remains up across eastern 
Canada and coastal low pressure strengthens off the Mid-Atlantic 
coast. This will lead to persistent onshore flow as a series of 
shortwave disturbances pivot around the coastal low offshore and the 
remnant stalled frontal boundary south/east of the region. The 
persistent northeast/east fetch off the Atlantic will yield 
continued cloudiness, minor to (potentially moderate) coastal 
flooding (along the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay), cool 
temperatures, and widespread shower chances. 

With a persistent wedge in place, expect highs to struggle to 
get out of the upper 50s and mid 60s through at least Friday. 
Overnight lows will fall into the 40s and 50s given the cool 
maritime airmass overhead.

Coastal low pressure will track northward toward the NJ/Long Island 
coast Friday into Saturday putting more subsidence over the region. 
This will allow for decreasing precipitation chances and rising 
temperatures with highs in the upper 60s and mid 70s. Even with that 
said, model discrepancies remain beyond Saturday as the coastal low 
looks to retrograde in the vicinity of the Mid-Atlantic coast.
